title: Coffee maker or espresso machine: safe teardown
summary: A drip coffee maker gives an aluminium heating tube with its warming plate, a thermostat, one-shot thermal fuses, heat-proof hoses and a switch. Espresso and pod machines add a pump, a solenoid valve and a control board. The dangers are mains wiring, scalding water and steam left inside, and thermal fuses, which must never be bridged.

steps.text: Unplug it, keep the plug where you can see it, and let it cool until the heater, the plate and any boiler are cool to touch. Empty the carafe, the water tank and the drip tray.
steps.warn: Espresso machines hold hot water under pressure while they run. Let them cool fully before you open anything.

steps.text: Commercial brewers have a tank of hot water inside that stays hot long after it is switched off. Switch off and unplug it, or switch off its breaker and tape it off if it is hard-wired (safety_mains_isolation), and shut off its water supply if it is plumbed in. Let the tank cool until the hood is cool to touch before you open it.
steps.warn: Water in the tank can scald. Feel the hood first.

steps.text: Turn the machine over on a towel. Undo the base screws: Phillips on some, tri-wing (Y1) or security Torx (T10) on others. Unclip the base plate and lift it off.
steps.warn: Leftover water will run out of the hoses. On a machine with a control board, touch nothing inside until the capacitor check in the next step.

steps.text: Programmable and pod machines have a control board. First check your meter works by reading a battery. Then measure DC volts across every large capacitor on it, discharge anything over about 30 V with the resistor tool from safety_discharge_capacitor (hold it on for 10 seconds), and measure again: under 1 V is safe. Then photograph the wiring.
Free the hoses from the heater: squeeze each spring clamp with pliers, slide it down the hose, and pull the hose off. Keep the hoses and clamps.

Find the thermal fuses: small metal cylinders on leads, in the wiring to the heater, sometimes two in a row. Read the marking on each and write it down. Loosen the crimp, or cut the leads as far from the body as you can, and don't bend or pull the leads near the body. A blown fuse means the machine overheated: find out why (stuck thermostat, dry or scaled heater) before you fit another, and never bridge a fuse or thermostat with wire.
Take the thermostat. It is held against the heater by a clip or by screws. Free it and keep the clip.
Undo the bracket screws over the heater and lift out the heating tube and warming plate together. Pull the plate off the tube if you want them apart.

Espresso and pod machines: first make sure the boiler or heater block is cool enough to hold, since it can keep scalding water and steam inside. Undo each hose slowly over a tray, with your face turned away, then undo the mounting and lift out the pump. Then take the solenoid valve and the heater block with its thermostats and fuses. Keep every hose.
Take the power switch and cut the cord off at the case, leaving it as long as you can.
Test each part with the meter (see the notes) and label it OK or BAD.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Heating tube and warming plate.** In some drip makers, one aluminium extrusion holds both a sheathed element (a coiled resistance wire packed in magnesium oxide) and the water tube. In one such design it is bent into a loop under the aluminium warming plate, with the thermostat and fuse clamped to it (US 4,748,901). In the Mr. Coffee DW13 the one heater warms both the water and the pot (iFixit DW13 teardown). At its own mains voltage it makes a small hot plate for one pot, or a heater for a trickle of water. Keep the thermostat and fuses on it. Run it only from an earthed supply, with its aluminium body earthed and its terminals covered, and on a residual-current (RCD or GFCI) protected circuit if you have one; a meter test can't prove a heater safe at mains voltage. Aluminium's low melting point keeps these heaters to about 900 W; a later patent proposes brazed stainless steel instead (US 6,327,429).
- **Thermal fuses.** Small one-shot cutoffs in the heater wiring; the Mr. Coffee 5-Cup has two, joined to each other (iFixit Mr. Coffee 5-Cup). The Bodum B.Over's is an SF169E rated 172 °C, 120 V, 15 A (iFixit Bodum B.Over). The Mr. Coffee 5-Cup uses SF214R0 parts (iFixit Mr. Coffee 5-Cup), which their maker rates at 216 °C (SCHOTT SEFUSE). Keep them as spares, tested and fitted as in "Reusing a thermal fuse" below.
- **Thermostat.** It keeps the water and the pot below a set temperature (iFixit DW13 teardown). A thermostat is a control, not a safety cutoff: keep one only if its marking shows its temperature, volts and amps, and never use it in place of a thermal fuse. BUNN says never to eliminate or bypass a limit thermostat (BUNN VP17 manual).
- **Hoses and clamps.** Heat-proof tubing that carried hot water, with spring clamps. Good for siphons, drip lines and short water runs.
- **Pump (espresso and pod machines).** The Breville BES870 has a 15 bar pump (Breville BES870 manual). The manual says nothing about the pump's type or voltage, so read the pump's own label before you power it. Never run it dry: the maker says never use the machine without water in the tank (Breville BES870 manual).
- **Solenoid valve (espresso and pod machines).** A water valve with an electric coil. Read the coil's voltage on its label before you power it.
- **Switch, cord and water tank.**

## Variations

- **Mr. Coffee DW13.** One heater under a metal pipe, a temperature regulator and a power switch. Water boils in the pipe and steam pushes it up the tube (iFixit DW13 teardown). The base comes off after eight Phillips screws, and the tubing is held to the heater by crimps (iFixit DW13 heating plate).
- **Mr. Coffee 5-Cup Mini Brew.** Three tri-wing (Y1) screws hold the base plate. Two thermal fuses are joined to each other, and the guide cuts them free at their mounts (iFixit Mr. Coffee 5-Cup).
- **Bodum B.Over.** The thermal fuse is crimped into place with a copper bead (iFixit Bodum B.Over).
- **Cuisinart DCC-1200.** Four T10 security Torx screws hold the bottom cover. The element plate is held by a clamp and two Phillips screws, and its contacts may be soldered (iFixit Cuisinart DCC-1200).
- **Espresso machines.** The Breville BES870 has a Thermocoil heater (a stainless steel water coil with PID temperature control), a 15 bar pump and a 2 L tank. It is rated 120 V, 60 Hz, 1,750 W, and is under pressure while brewing (Breville BES870 manual).
- **Commercial brewers.** The BUNN VP17 keeps a tank of hot water. Its tank heater is inside the tank, fixed to the lid, and a limit thermostat sits on the lid. The maker says never to remove or bypass that limit thermostat (BUNN VP17 manual).

## Testing what you got out

Take at least one wire off each part before you test it (see test_continuity).

- **Heater.** Set the meter to ohms. Expected ohms are about volts × volts ÷ watts, using the rating label: a 120 V, 900 W heater reads about 16 Ω. OL means it is burnt out. Then test from each terminal to the aluminium body: anything but OL means a short, so scrap it. BUNN also has you check its tank heater for continuity and look for cracks in the sheath (BUNN VP17 manual).
- **Thermal fuses.** Test each one separately. A good fuse reads close to 0 Ω; OL means it has blown (iFixit Bodum B.Over). They can't be reset (iFixit Mr. Coffee 5-Cup).
- **Thermostat.** With its wires off, check for continuity across its terminals, as BUNN does for its limit thermostat (BUNN VP17 manual).
- **Switch.** Close to 0 Ω on, OL off.
- **Pump and valve coils.** A steady number of ohms, not OL.

## Reusing a thermal fuse

Fit one with the same temperature rating, and use it only below its rated volts and amps. It is not a current fuse (SCHOTT SEFUSE). A fuse taken out of a machine has an unknown history: SCHOTT says a link can be changed by force or heat, that long time near its rating shrinks the thermal pellet for good, and that a deformed case may make it open too early or not at all (SCHOTT SEFUSE). Reuse only one with an undamaged body and straight leads. A continuity test shows only that it has not opened, not that it will open at its rated temperature, so treat a salvaged one as a last resort anywhere a failure could start a fire. Keep its body insulated from other metal, since it sits at circuit voltage, and check a crimped joint reads close to 0 Ω: a poor joint heats up and can open the fuse (SCHOTT SEFUSE). Join it by crimping, like the Bodum, or by soldering, at least 5 mm from the body. When soldering, grip the lead with pliers between the joint and the body and solder in short bursts, or the heat can blow it. Bend leads at least 3 mm from the body, never at the root, and don't twist them (SCHOTT SEFUSE). Never bridge a fuse or thermostat with wire.

## What to leave

- Heaters thick with scale inside, or with cracked sheaths.
- Cracked glass carafes.
- Control boards, unless you want the relays.
